Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

issues.item: Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs
issues.explanation: These trigger items are not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of mugging/robbery. Physical affection such as hugs is difficult to connect to robbery-related threat activation without any supporting appraisal, memory, or strategy content, and it conflicts with the otherwise stranger/sudden-movement threat profile. Crash imagery is more characteristic of road traffic trauma than robbery and lacks any plausible link to the reported threat items.

issues.item: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: The trigger item about cars being hit in an accident is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of mugging/robbery. The other trigger and threat items coherently suggest interpersonal danger and hypervigilance around strangers/crowding, but crash imagery points to a motor vehicle trauma theme that is not reflected elsewhere in the profile or in the cognitive formulation. This is more than unusual; it appears to reference a different trauma context.

vignette:
At 76, Rajesh Patel had spent decades working as an electrician, the kind of man who was used to entering other people’s buildings before sunrise, carrying his tools through service hallways and apartment basements, and trusting his hands to know what to do in dim light. The robbery happened on an evening that had felt routine. He had finished a small repair job later than expected and was making his way home with his tool bag when a man came up too close, too quickly. Rajesh remembered the abruptness of it most clearly: the stranger’s body entering his space without warning, a sharp movement of an arm, the demand for his wallet and bag delivered with the heavy smell of alcohol on the man’s breath. It was not only the threat itself that stayed with him, but the way the man swayed slightly and then lunged again when Rajesh hesitated, making every motion feel unpredictable. Even now, when he spoke about it, he described that moment as one in which he stopped feeling he could read what another person might do next.

In the days afterward, Rajesh told his wife he was lucky to have come home alive and tried to carry on. He went back to work, still taking jobs in apartment buildings and small stores, still riding elevators and walking through shared corridors with coils of wire over his shoulder. But ordinary moments began to acquire a charged quality. If a tenant stepped out suddenly from a doorway while he was working in a hallway, his whole body snapped to attention before he had time to think. If someone on a subway platform shifted direction quickly or reached into a pocket too fast, Rajesh found himself bracing, watching the hands, measuring the distance between them. Strangers no longer felt neutral to him. A person approaching to ask a simple question could make him tense immediately, as though every unfamiliar face carried the possibility of another sudden demand.

Crowded places became especially difficult. At first he only noticed that he was more irritable in busy grocery aisles or on packed trains, but over time he began arranging his life around avoiding them. He sent his wife or adult children to shop on weekends and chose errands only at quiet hours. On workdays, if a building lobby was full of residents coming and going, Rajesh would wait outside longer than necessary, pretending to check paperwork until the space cleared. In tightly packed places he felt trapped by too many bodies and too many movements he could not track all at once. The problem was not noise or social discomfort; it was the sense that danger could come from any direction before he could prepare himself.

Certain sensory moments cut through him with particular force. The smell of alcohol was the worst. Passing a group outside a liquor store, or catching stale beer on someone’s clothing in an elevator, could bring back the feeling of that man leaning in, unsteady and close. He did not describe this as a deliberate recollection so much as a sudden return of the atmosphere of the robbery. Night was also harder than day. Rajesh had come to feel that darkness itself reduced his margin for safety. After sunset he checked locks repeatedly and looked through windows before opening the door, even in his own neighborhood where he had lived for years. If he heard footsteps outside late at night, he stayed alert long after the sound had passed. He slept lightly, and when he woke from nightmares he was not immediately reassured by being at home beside his wife. The residue of the dream stayed on him, and for several minutes he felt as if he were still in the moment of being confronted, heart pounding, listening for movement in the house.

These changes accumulated quietly. His wife noticed that he no longer wanted to attend family gatherings held in crowded banquet halls and that he refused evening invitations unless someone could drive him door to door. At work he became more selective, turning down jobs that would keep him late or take him into busy commercial spaces. He was embarrassed by this. Rajesh had always seen himself as practical and steady, and now he found himself scanning every stranger who came toward him, feeling his body harden at sudden gestures that other people barely registered.

What finally brought him to seek help was not a new assault but the narrowing of his world. After waking from another nightmare and sitting upright in bed, fully alert to imagined danger in the darkened room, he realized how little ease he felt anymore, especially at night. A few days later, while crossing a crowded building lobby for a service call, a man turned abruptly toward him and Rajesh jerked back so sharply that he dropped part of his toolkit. He was shaken by how immediate the reaction was and by how exposed he felt in front of others. Coming to treatment, he said he was afraid that he would never again feel ordinary around people, that every approach by a stranger would keep seeming like the beginning of something violent. What he hoped for, more simply, was to walk into his own workspaces and his own neighborhood without being on guard all the time.
